analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying or restricting coverage for pre-existing conditions nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have guaranteed health coverage to people with pre-existing conditions, was introduced in 1989 with 18 cosponsors but never got a vote, dying in a House subcommittee after hearings.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write national minimum rules for how health plans treat people with pre-existing conditions, then required every state to adopt and enforce them. Plans could not exclude, terminate, or limit coverage because someone was already sick, and could not set premiums or out-of-pocket charges based on that person's claims history. Plans that broke the rules would face federal fines of $100 per enrolled person per day and could be sued for damages by the people they hurt.
analysis.who_benefits: People with pre-existing conditions — anyone with cancer, diabetes, heart disease, a disability, or any other health condition — who could be denied coverage, charged more, dropped mid-illness, or priced out under existing insurance practices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit health plan sponsors from excluding, terminating, or limiting any individual's coverage because of a pre-existing condition, defined broadly as any disease, disability, disorder, impairment, or other health condition.

It would bar plans from setting premiums, deductibles, copayments, or coinsurance based on the number or amount of claims a person had submitted, and would require that charges be based on current medical and financial data rather than a sick person's history.

Every state would have to adopt and enforce the standards through penalties, with a designated office to investigate complaints and help the public with health benefits questions, and the Secretary could withdraw certification from states that failed to enforce them.

Noncompliant plans would face a federal civil penalty of $100 per enrolled individual per day and would be liable to individuals and their families for damages, including health care costs caused by the denial of coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance companies and other plan sponsors — employers and insurers running health benefit plans — would bear the cost of covering sick enrollees at community-like rates instead of excluding or surcharging them, plus fines and damage liability for violations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and other plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: The bill set no funding mechanism for the state enforcement offices it required and left states to legislate and fund compliance within a tight timeline, which small states and state legislatures argued was a heavy unfunded mandate style burden.

Insurers and employer plan sponsors warned that forced coverage of pre-existing conditions without a broader risk pool would raise premiums for everyone else, since the healthy would subsidize the sick; the bill allowed uniform waiting and open-enrollment periods but did not create a pool or subsidy to spread those costs.

The bill exempted plan sponsors in federally certified states from the federal civil penalty entirely, meaning enforcement would depend on the rigor of each state's insurance regulator, with uneven protection across the country.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly tens of millions of Americans with a health condition that made them uninsurable or unaffordably insured, the gain — guaranteed coverage at regulated cost-sharing — was substantial and direct. The main costs fell on insurers and plan sponsors, with some risk that premiums for healthy enrollees would rise since the bill spread costs through the private market without a subsidy or pool. The design relied on state enforcement rather than federal policing, a real weakness, but it addressed one of the most concrete and well-documented failures of the pre-ACA insurance market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress; it got a hearing in September 1990 but was never reported out, never reached the House floor, and expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Doug Walgren (D-PA) introduced the bill on June 14, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On July 5, 1989, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness, where it remained.
Between July 19, 1990 and later in 1990, 18 members — 15 Democrats and 3 Republicans — signed on as cosponsors, including Reps. Nancy Pelosi and Christopher Shays.
The subcommittee held hearings on September 19, 1990, but the bill was never reported to the full committee and never received a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and plan sponsors, who avoided a national requirement to cover pre-existing conditions and the fines and damages that came with it. People with pre-existing conditions gained nothing; the country's insurance rules on this were not fixed until the 2010 Affordable Care Act over a decade later.

for.name: Rep. Doug Walgren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole original sponsor.

for.name: 15 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Nancy Pelosi, Jim McDermott, and Marcy Kaptur.

for.name: 3 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. Christopher Shays of Connecticut.

for.name: Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on September 19, 1990, its only action beyond referral.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup in the roughly 19 months it had jurisdiction over it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; the support that did appear skewed heavily Democratic, with 15 of the 18 cosponsors Democrats and 3 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers to cover people with pre-existing conditions at regulated cost-sharing and banned pricing based on claims history, directly attacking underwriting practices that keep sick people out of coverage. Its penalties ($100 per enrollee per day) and damages liability made noncompliance costly.

industries.industry: Employer health plan sponsors (including self-insured plans)
industries.note: 'Sponsor' was defined broadly to cover any entity providing a health benefit plan, so employers running plans would also have faced the coverage mandates, fines, and damages liability. Their relief at the bill's death was the same as insurers': no obligation to cover sick enrollees.

States would have gained a mandate to adopt and enforce national standards plus a new complaint-handling office, a real administrative and legislative burden with no federal funding attached — but their residents gained enforceable coverage protections.
